results.title: Local consequence in a normal modal logic
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ and $\Gamma$ be sets of modal formulas. The local consequences of the hypotheses $\Gamma$ in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$ form the least set of modal formulas that contains every member of $\Gamma$ and every theorem of $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$ and is closed under modus ponens: whenever it contains $\varphi \to \psi$ and $\varphi$, it contains $\psi$.

results.title: Extra axioms of the modal logic K
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The set of extra axioms of the normal modal logic K is the empty set of modal formulas over a given type of atoms; that is, K adds no axioms to the propositional axioms and the distribution axiom.

results.title: Extra axioms of T
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The extra axioms of the modal logic T are the formulas $\Box\varphi \to \varphi$ (axiom T), for all modal formulas $\varphi$.

results.title: Extra axioms of S4
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The extra axioms of the modal logic S4 are the formulas $\Box\varphi \to \varphi$ (axiom T) and $\Box\varphi \to \Box\Box\varphi$ (axiom 4), for all modal formulas $\varphi$.

results.title: Extra axioms of S5
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a modal formula $\varphi$, write $\Diamond\varphi$ for $\neg\Box\neg\varphi$. The extra axioms of the modal logic S5 are the formulas $\Box\varphi \to \varphi$ (axiom T) and $\Diamond\varphi \to \Box\Diamond\varphi$ (axiom 5), for all modal formulas $\varphi$.

results.title: Self-implication is a theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas. For every modal formula $\varphi$, the formula $\varphi \to \varphi$ is a theorem of the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: Monotonicity of theorems in the extra axioms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda \subseteq \Lambda'$ be sets of modal formulas. Every theorem of the normal modal logic $\mathrm{K} \oplus \Lambda$ is a theorem of $\mathrm{K} \oplus \Lambda'$.

results.title: Monotonicity of local consequence in the hypotheses
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$, $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be sets of modal formulas with $\Gamma \subseteq \Delta$. If a formula $\varphi$ is a local consequence of the hypotheses $\Gamma$ in the normal modal logic $\mathrm{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then $\varphi$ is a local consequence of the hypotheses $\Delta$ in $\mathrm{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: Transitivity of local consequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas and let $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be sets of formulas such that every formula of $\Delta$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$ in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$. If a formula $\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Delta$ in $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then $\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$ in $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: The deduction theorem for local modal consequence, forward direction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ and $\Gamma$ be sets of modal formulas and let $\varphi$, $\psi$ be modal formulas. If $\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma \cup \{\psi\}$ in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then $\psi \to \varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$ in $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: The deduction theorem for local modal consequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ and $\Gamma$ be sets of modal formulas and let $\varphi$, $\psi$ be modal formulas. In the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, $\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma \cup \{\psi\}$ if and only if $\psi \to \varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$.

results.title: Consequences of no hypotheses are the theorems
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas. A modal formula $\varphi$ is a local consequence of the empty set of hypotheses in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$ if and only if $\varphi$ is a theorem of $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: Compactness of local modal consequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ and $\Gamma$ be sets of modal formulas. If a modal formula $\varphi$ is a local consequence of the hypotheses $\Gamma$ in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then there is a finite set $\Delta \subseteq \Gamma$ such that $\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Delta$ in $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: Ex falso quodlibet
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas and $\Gamma$ a set of hypotheses. If $\bot$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$ in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then every formula $\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$ in $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: Contradiction yields falsity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ and $\Gamma$ be sets of modal formulas and let $\varphi$ be a modal formula. If both $\varphi$ and its negation $\neg\varphi$ are local consequences of the hypotheses $\Gamma$ in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then so is $\bot$.

results.title: Proof by contradiction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas, $\Gamma$ a set of hypotheses and $\varphi$ a formula. If $\bot$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma \cup \{\neg\varphi\}$ in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then $\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$ in $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: Negation introduction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ and $\Gamma$ be sets of modal formulas and $\varphi$ a formula. If $\bot$ is a local consequence of the hypotheses $\Gamma \cup \{\varphi\}$ in the normal modal logic $\mathrm{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then $\neg\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$ in $\mathrm{K} \oplus \Lambda$, where $\neg\varphi$ abbreviates $\varphi \to \bot$.

results.title: Hypothetical syllogism
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ and $\Gamma$ be sets of modal formulas and let $\varphi$, $\psi$, $\chi$ be modal formulas. If $\varphi \to \psi$ and $\psi \to \chi$ are local consequences of the hypotheses $\Gamma$ in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then so is $\varphi \to \chi$.

results.title: Local consequences of theorems are theorems
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas and let $\Gamma$ be a set of formulas each of which is a theorem of the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$. If a formula $\varphi$ is a local consequence of $\Gamma$ in $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then $\varphi$ is a theorem of $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: The monotonicity rule for necessity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas and let $\varphi$, $\psi$ be modal formulas. If $\varphi \to \psi$ is a theorem of the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then so is $\Box\varphi \to \Box\psi$.

results.title: Soundness of modal Hilbert systems for Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas and $M$ a Kripke model in which every formula of $\Lambda$ is valid. Then every formula derivable in $K \oplus \Lambda$ (from the propositional axioms, the distribution axiom and the members of $\Lambda$ by modus ponens and necessitation) is valid in $M$, that is, it holds at every world of $M$.

results.title: Local soundness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\Lambda$ a set of modal formulas each of which is valid in $M$. If a formula $\varphi$ is a local consequence of a set $\Gamma$ of formulas in the normal modal logic $\mathbf{K} \oplus \Lambda$, then $\varphi$ holds at every world of $M$ at which every formula of $\Gamma$ holds.

results.title: Soundness of K for Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every theorem of the modal logic K is valid in every Kripke model: if a formula $\varphi$ is derivable in K, then $\varphi$ holds at every world of every Kripke model $M$.

results.title: Soundness of T for reflexive Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the accessibility relation of a Kripke model $M$ is reflexive, then every formula derivable in the modal logic T is valid in $M$, that is, it holds at every world of $M$.

results.title: Soundness of S4 for reflexive transitive Kripke models
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the accessibility relation of a Kripke model $M$ is reflexive and transitive, then every formula derivable in the modal logic S4 is valid in $M$, that is, it holds at every world of $M$.

results.title: Soundness of S5 for Kripke models with an equivalence relation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the accessibility relation of a Kripke model $M$ is an equivalence relation, then every formula derivable in the modal logic S5 is valid in $M$, that is, it holds at every world of $M$.

results.title: The one-world Kripke model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For any type of atoms, the one-world Kripke model has a single world, which sees itself, and every atom is false at that world.

results.title: The one-world model has an equivalence relation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The accessibility relation of the one-world Kripke model, whose single world sees itself and at which every atom is false, is an equivalence relation.

results.title: Consistency of normal modal logics
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Lambda$ be a set of modal formulas each of which is valid in the one-world Kripke model whose world sees itself and in which every atom is false. Then $\bot$ is not a theorem of the normal modal logic $\mathrm{K} \oplus \Lambda$.

results.title: Consistency of S4
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every type of atoms, $\bot$ is not a theorem of the normal modal logic S4, whose extra axioms are the formulas $\Box\varphi \to \varphi$ and $\Box\varphi \to \Box\Box\varphi$.

results.title: Consistency of T
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every type of atoms, $\bot$ is not a theorem of the normal modal logic T, whose extra axioms are the formulas $\Box\varphi \to \varphi$.

results.title: Partitions of groups of singular cardinality (Kourovka 13.45)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that every infinite group $G$ whose cardinality $\mathfrak{m} = |G|$ is singular (not regular) can be split into two disjoint sets $A_1$ and $A_2$ with $A_1 \cup A_2 = G$ such that $A_1 F \ne G$ and $A_2 F \ne G$ for every subset $F \subseteq G$ with $|F| < \mathfrak{m}$, where $A F = \{a f : a \in A, f \in F\}$.

results.title: Some group of singular cardinality has no such partition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an infinite group $G$ whose cardinality $\mathfrak{m} = |G|$ is singular (not regular) such that for all disjoint sets $A_1$ and $A_2$ with $A_1 \cup A_2 = G$ there is a subset $F \subseteq G$ with $|F| < \mathfrak{m}$ and $A_1 F = G$ or $A_2 F = G$, where $A F = \{a f : a \in A, f \in F\}$. That is, the statement of Kourovka Problem 13.45 fails.

results.title: Trace is additive over an invariant subspace
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $K$, let $e$ be a linear endomorphism of $V$, and let $W$ be a subspace of $V$ with $e(W) \subseteq W$. Then the trace of $e$ equals the trace of the restriction $e|_W$ of $e$ to $W$ plus the trace of the endomorphism $\bar e$ of the quotient $V/W$ induced by $e$: $\operatorname{tr}(e) = \operatorname{tr}(e|_W) + \operatorname{tr}(\bar e)$.

results.title: Trace splits along a surjective intertwining map
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $K$, let $W$ be a vector space over $K$, and let $q : V \to W$ be a surjective linear map. If $f$ is a linear endomorphism of $V$ and $g$ a linear endomorphism of $W$ with $q \circ f = g \circ q$, then $f$ maps $\ker q$ into itself, and the trace of $f$ equals the trace of the restriction $f|_{\ker q}$ of $f$ to $\ker q$ plus the trace of $g$.

results.title: Periodicity of Tate cohomology for finite cyclic groups
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $G$ a finite cyclic group and $A$ a representation of $G$ over $R$. Then for every integer $n$, the Tate cohomology groups $\hat{H}^n(G, A)$ and $\hat{H}^{n+2}(G, A)$ are isomorphic as $R$-modules.

results.title: Cardinality of Tate cohomology
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ and $n$ an integer. This is the cardinality of the Tate cohomology group $\hat H^n(G, M)$, as a cardinal number (possibly infinite).

results.title: Cardinality of Tate homology
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$. For an integer $n$, the cardinality $h_n(M)$ of the degree-$n$ Tate homology of $M$ is defined as the cardinal number of the Tate cohomology group $\hat H^{-n-1}(G, M)$, following the convention $\hat H_n = \hat H^{-n-1}$.

results.title: Cardinality of Tate homology in degree zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$. The cardinality of the degree-$0$ Tate homology of $M$ equals the cardinality of the Tate cohomology group $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$.

results.title: Cardinality of finite Tate cohomology as a natural number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ and $n$ an integer such that the Tate cohomology group $\hat H^n(G, M)$ is finite. Then the cardinality of $\hat H^n(G, M)$ equals its number of elements, a natural number viewed as a cardinal number.

results.title: Finiteness hypothesis for the Herbrand quotient
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$. The representation $M$ satisfies the Herbrand finiteness hypothesis when its Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are both finite.

results.title: Herbrand quotient
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. The Herbrand quotient of $M$ is the rational number $h(M) = |\hat H^0(G, M)| / |\hat H^{-1}(G, M)|$, where $|X|$ is the number of elements of $X$.

results.title: Herbrand quotient as a ratio of orders
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. Then the Herbrand quotient of $M$ equals the rational number $|\hat H^0(G, M)| / |\hat H^{-1}(G, M)|$, where $|X|$ is the number of elements of $X$.

results.title: The denominator of the Herbrand quotient is positive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. Then the number of elements of $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ is positive.

results.title: The denominator of the Herbrand quotient is nonzero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. Then the number of elements of $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ is nonzero.

results.title: Positivity of the Herbrand quotient
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $R$ a commutative ring and $M$ an $R$-linear representation of $G$ whose Tate cohomology groups $\hat H^0(G, M)$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, M)$ are finite. Then the Herbrand quotient of $M$ is strictly positive.

results.title: Regularity of a fraction at an evaluation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $A$ and $K$ be commutative rings and $\mathrm{ev} : A \to K$ a ring homomorphism. An element $r$ of the total ring of fractions of $A$ (its localization at the non-zero-divisors) is regular at $\mathrm{ev}$ when there is some $g \in A$ with $\mathrm{ev}(g) \neq 0$ such that $g r$ lies in the image of $A$ in its total ring of fractions.

results.title: Elements of the base ring are regular
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $K$ a nontrivial commutative ring. For every ring homomorphism $\mathrm{ev} : A \to K$ and every $a \in A$, the image of $a$ in the total ring of fractions of $A$ is regular at $\mathrm{ev}$.

results.title: Zero is regular
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $K$ a nontrivial commutative ring. For every ring homomorphism $\mathrm{ev} : A \to K$, the element $0$ of the total ring of fractions of $A$ is regular at $\mathrm{ev}$.

results.title: One is regular
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $K$ a nontrivial commutative ring. For every ring homomorphism $\mathrm{ev} : A \to K$, the element $1$ of the total ring of fractions of $A$ is regular at $\mathrm{ev}$.

results.title: Affine coordinate ring
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field, $\sigma$ an index set and $X \subseteq K^\sigma$ a set of points. The affine coordinate ring of $X$ is the quotient $K[x_i : i \in \sigma] / I(X)$ of the polynomial ring over $K$ in variables indexed by $\sigma$ by the vanishing ideal $I(X)$, the ideal of all polynomials that vanish at every point of $X$.

results.title: Evaluation at a point of an affine set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field, $\sigma$ an index set and $X \subseteq K^\sigma$ a set of points. For a point $P \in X$, evaluation at $P$ is the ring homomorphism from the affine coordinate ring of $X$ to $K$ that sends the residue class of a polynomial $f$ to $f(P)$; it is well defined because every polynomial in the vanishing ideal of $X$ vanishes at $P$.

results.title: Evaluating a residue class
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field, $\sigma$ an index set, $X \subseteq K^\sigma$ a set of points and $P \in X$. For every polynomial $f$ over $K$ in variables indexed by $\sigma$, evaluating the residue class of $f$ in the affine coordinate ring of $X$ at $P$ gives $f(P)$.

results.title: Regularity of a rational function at a point
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field, $\sigma$ an index set and $X \subseteq K^\sigma$ a set of points whose affine coordinate ring $A$ is an integral domain. A rational function on $X$ is an element $r$ of the field of fractions of $A$; it is regular at a point $P \in X$ when there is some $g \in A$ whose value $g(P)$ under evaluation at $P$ is nonzero such that $g r$ lies in the image of $A$ in its field of fractions.

results.title: Elements of the coordinate ring are regular
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field, $\sigma$ an index set and $X \subseteq K^\sigma$ a set of points whose affine coordinate ring $A$ is an integral domain. For every $a \in A$ and every point $P \in X$, the image of $a$ in the field of fractions of $A$ is a rational function on $X$ that is regular at $P$.

results.summary: Let $V$ be a combinatorial subspace of $\alpha^\iota$ with parameter set $\eta$, viewed as its map $x \mapsto V(x)$ from parameter values to points, and let $l$ be a combinatorial line in $\alpha^\eta$, with $l(a)$ the point of $l$ whose free coordinates equal $a$. Then for every $a \in \alpha$, the point at $a$ of the image line $V_* l$ is $V(l(a))$.

results.title: Images of lines under composite subspaces
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be a combinatorial subspace of $\alpha^\iota$ with parameter set $\eta$, let $W$ be a combinatorial subspace of $\alpha^\eta$ with parameter set $\eta'$, and let $l$ be a combinatorial line in $\alpha^{\eta'}$. Then the image of $l$ under the composite $V \circ W$ equals the image under $V$ of the image of $l$ under $W$, that is, $(V \circ W)_* l = V_*(W_* l)$.

results.title: Minimal permutations of length two more than their number of descents
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Closed segment in the plane
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For points $a$ and $b$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, the closed segment from $a$ to $b$ is the set of points $a + t(b - a)$ with $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $0 \le t \le 1$.

results.title: Straight-line planar graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A simple graph $G$ with vertex set $V$ is straight-line planar if either $V$ is empty or there is an injective map $f$ from $V$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that, for any two different edges $vw$ and $xy$ of $G$, the closed segment from $f(v)$ to $f(w)$ and the closed segment from $f(x)$ to $f(y)$ meet only in points of $\{f(v), f(w)\} \cap \{f(x), f(y)\}$.

results.title: Occurrence list of a CNF formula
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a CNF formula $\varphi = (C_1, \dots, C_m)$, the occurrence list of $\varphi$ is the list of the variable indices of its literals, in order: the variables of the literals of $C_1$ in order, then those of $C_2$, and so on up to $C_m$. Duplicates are kept, so a variable appears once for each literal in which it occurs.

results.title: Witness lookup
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Clause check against a witness
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $N$ of natural numbers, a list $w$ of booleans and a CNF clause $C$, the check of $C$ against $N$ and $w$ is the timed computation (a returned boolean together with a natural-number cost) that scans the literals $(x, b)$ of $C$ in order: for each it charges one tick, then looks up $x$ in $N$ and $w$, paying the cost of the lookup, and returns true if the value found equals the polarity $b$; otherwise…

results.title: Formula check against a witness
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $N$ of natural numbers, a list $w$ of booleans and a CNF formula $\varphi$, the check of $\varphi$ against $N$ and $w$ is the timed computation that runs the clause check against $N$ and $w$ on the clauses of $\varphi$ in order, adding up their costs, and returns false as soon as one of them returns false. If every clause check returns true, in particular if $\varphi$ has no clauses, it returns true.

results.title: The SAT verifier
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The SAT verifier takes a pair $(x, w)$ of lists of Booleans, an input $x$ and a witness $w$, and returns a Boolean together with a declared time cost. If the complete CNF decoder fails on $x$, it returns false at cost $0$. If $x$ decodes to a CNF formula $\varphi$, it returns the result and the cost of the CNF check of $\varphi$ against the witness $w$ and the occurrence list of $\varphi$, so that $w$ is read as…

results.title: Cost bound for witness lookup
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $N$ of natural numbers, every list $w$ of booleans and every natural number $x$, the cost of looking up $x$ in $N$ and $w$ is at most the length of $N$.

results.title: Lookup in the witness of an assignment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $v$ be a function from the natural numbers to the booleans, $N = (n_1, \dots, n_k)$ a list of natural numbers and $x$ a natural number. Looking up $x$ in $N$ and the list $(v(n_1), \dots, v(n_k))$ returns $v(x)$ if $x$ occurs in $N$, and false otherwise.

results.title: Correctness of the witness clause check
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $N$ be a list of natural numbers, $w$ a list of booleans and $C$ a CNF clause. The check of $C$ against $N$ and $w$ returns true if and only if $C$ is satisfied by the assignment that sends each natural number $x$ to the value returned by looking up $x$ in $N$ and $w$.

results.title: Cost bound for the witness clause check
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $N$ be a list of natural numbers, $w$ a list of booleans and $C$ a CNF clause, viewed as a list of $\ell$ literals (repetitions counted). The cost of checking $C$ against $N$ and $w$ is at most $\ell \cdot (|N| + 1)$, where $|N|$ is the length of $N$.

results.title: Correctness of the witness formula check
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $N$ be a list of natural numbers, $w$ a list of booleans and $\varphi$ a CNF formula. The check of $\varphi$ against $N$ and $w$ returns true if and only if $\varphi$ is satisfied by the assignment that sends each natural number $x$ to the value returned by looking up $x$ in $N$ and $w$.

results.title: Cost bound for the witness formula check
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $N$ be a list of natural numbers, $w$ a list of booleans and $\varphi$ a CNF formula, and let $L$ be the sum of the lengths of the clauses of $\varphi$ (its total number of literals). The cost of checking $\varphi$ against $N$ and $w$ is at most $L \cdot (|N| + 1)$, where $|N|$ is the length of $N$.

results.title: Length of the occurrence list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every CNF formula $\varphi$, the length of the occurrence list of $\varphi$ equals the total number of literals of $\varphi$, that is, the sum over the clauses of $\varphi$ of their lengths.

results.title: Variables of a formula occur in its occurrence list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula, $C$ a clause of $\varphi$ and $(x, b)$ a literal of $C$. Then $x$ belongs to the list of variables occurring in $\varphi$.

results.title: The literal count is at most the code length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every CNF formula $\varphi$, the sum over the clauses of $\varphi$ of their lengths (the total number of literals of $\varphi$) is at most the length of the length-prefixed binary code of $\varphi$.

results.title: The SAT verifier rejects undecodable inputs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all lists of Booleans $x$ and $w$, if the complete CNF decoder fails on $x$, then the SAT verifier on $(x, w)$ returns false at declared time cost $0$.

results.title: The SAT verifier on a decodable input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all lists of Booleans $x$ and $w$ and every CNF formula $\varphi$, if the complete CNF decoder returns $\varphi$ on $x$, then the SAT verifier on $(x, w)$ coincides with the CNF check of $\varphi$ against the witness $w$ and the occurrence list of $\varphi$: both the returned Boolean and the declared time cost are the same.

results.title: Declared time bound of the SAT verifier
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all lists of Booleans $x$ (the input) and $w$ (the witness), the declared time cost of the SAT verifier on $(x, w)$ is at most $N^2 + N$, where $N = |x| + |w|$ is the sum of their lengths.

results.title: The SAT verifier has polynomial declared time
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a polynomial $q$ with natural number coefficients such that for all lists of Booleans $x$ (the input) and $w$ (the witness), the declared time cost of the SAT verifier on $(x, w)$ is at most $q(|x| + |w|)$.

results.title: The SAT verifier verifies SAT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The SAT verifier verifies the SAT decision problem with witness bound the polynomial $X$: for every list $x$ of Booleans, $x$ encodes a satisfiable CNF formula if and only if there is a list $w$ of Booleans, of length at most the length of $x$, such that the SAT verifier on $(x, w)$ returns true.

results.title: SAT is in NP if its verifier is polynomial-time
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the function sending a pair $(x, w)$ of lists of Booleans to the Boolean returned by the SAT verifier on $(x, w)$ is polynomial-time computable, by a multi-stack Turing machine under the canonical bitstring encodings, then the SAT decision problem belongs to NP.

results.title: Stack alphabet of the SAT verifier
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The symbols of the token and table stacks are a name bit $b$ for each boolean $b$, a polarity marker for each polarity $p$, a clause end marker, a value marker for each boolean $b$, and a dead marker. Equality of symbols is decidable.

results.title: Reading a symbol as a name bit
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A symbol of the token and table stacks that is the name bit $b$ reads as the bit $b$; every other symbol reads as no bit, and so ends a name block.

results.title: Tokens of a literal
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a literal $(n, p)$ with variable index $n$ and polarity $p$, the token list is one bit symbol for each bit of the canonical binary representation of $n$ (least significant bit first, empty for $n = 0$), in order, followed by the polarity marker symbol for $p$.

results.title: Tokens of a clause
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The tokens of a CNF clause are the tokens of its literals, in order, followed by the clause-end symbol.

results.title: Token sequence of a CNF formula
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a CNF formula $\varphi$ with clauses $C_1, \dots, C_k$ (in order), the token sequence of $\varphi$ is the concatenation of the token sequences of $C_1, \dots, C_k$. The token sequence of a clause is the concatenation of the token sequences of its literals, in order, followed by a clause-end symbol; the token sequence of a literal with variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and polarity $p$ is the bits of the binary…

results.title: Table entries
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A table entry is a pair of a name, which is a list of bits, and an optional bit, its value; the value is absent for occurrences past the end of the witness.

results.title: Closing marker of a table entry
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The marker closing a table entry whose value is the boolean $b$ is the value symbol for $b$; for an entry with no value it is the dead symbol.

results.title: Symbols of a table entry
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The symbols of a table entry with name $q$ and value $v$ are the bits of $q$ as name-bit symbols, in order, followed by one closing marker: the value marker of $b$ if $v$ is a bit $b$, and the dead marker if $v$ is absent.

results.title: Table stack of an entry list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write each table entry as one bit symbol per bit of its name followed by its closing marker (the value symbol for its value, or the dead symbol if it has no value), and concatenate these in the order of the list. The table stack is the reverse of this sequence, with the head as the top of the stack, so the first entry lies at the bottom.

results.title: Occurrence table of a list of variables
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given natural numbers $n_0, \dots, n_{k-1}$ and a list $w$ of bits, the occurrence table is the list of $k$ table entries whose $i$-th entry has as name the binary code of $n_i$ (Mathlib's encoding of natural numbers as bit lists) and as value the bit $w_i$ if $i$ is less than the length of $w$, and no value otherwise.

results.title: Occurrence table of a formula and a witness
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula, $w$ a list of booleans, and $n_0, \dots, n_{k-1}$ the variable indices of the literals of $\varphi$ in reading order, with repetitions. The occurrence table is the list of $k$ entries whose $i$-th entry pairs the binary name of $n_i$ (its canonical binary representation, least significant bit first, empty for $0$) with the value $w_i$ if $i$ is less than the length of $w$, and with…

results.title: Live value of a name in a table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list of table entries, each pairing a name (a bit string) with either a boolean value or no value, and a bit string $q$, the live value of $q$ is the value of the first entry whose name is $q$ and which carries a value, or false if there is no such entry.

results.title: Clause check against an occurrence table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a CNF formula $\varphi$ and a list $es$ of table entries, the clause check is true exactly when every clause of $\varphi$ contains a literal $(x, p)$ whose live value equals its polarity $p$. Here the live value of $x$ is the value of the first entry of $es$ that is named by the binary code of $x$ and has a value, and false if there is no such entry.

results.title: Tokenizer of the SAT verifier
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given bit strings $x$ and $w$, the tokenizer rejects (returns no result) if $x$ does not decode to a CNF formula. If $x$ decodes to a formula $\varphi$, it returns the pair consisting of the token stack, the reverse of the tokens of $\varphi$ in reading order, and the table stack of the occurrence table of $\varphi$ and $w$.

results.title: The binary code of natural numbers is injective
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $m$ and $n$, the binary codes of $m$ and $n$ (Mathlib's encoding of natural numbers as bit lists) are equal if and only if $m = n$.

results.title: Canonical binary names
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $l$ of bits, encoding the natural number that $l$ decodes to (Mathlib's binary code of natural numbers, least significant bit first) gives back $l$ if and only if $l$ is empty or its last bit is true.

results.title: The clause check on the occurrence table is the formula check
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every CNF formula $\varphi$ and every list $w$ of bits, the clause check of $\varphi$ against the occurrence table of $\varphi$ and $w$ equals the value returned (ignoring the time count) by the formula check of $\varphi$ against $w$ that uses the variable occurrences of $\varphi$, in order, as its variable list.

results.title: The SAT verifier's answer through the occurrence table
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all lists $x$ and $w$ of bits, the value returned by the SAT verifier on $(x, w)$, ignoring the time count, is false if the complete length-prefixed CNF decoder fails on $x$, and is the clause check of $\varphi$ against the occurrence table of $\varphi$ and $w$ if $x$ decodes to the CNF formula $\varphi$.

results.title: A clause has at most as many tokens as code bits
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every CNF clause $C$, the number of tokens of $C$ is at most the length of the binary code of $C$.

results.title: Token count is bounded by the encoding length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every CNF formula $\varphi$, the number of tokens of $\varphi$ is at most the length of the binary encoding of $\varphi$.

results.title: Stacks of the lookup machine
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The lookup machine has six stacks: the query stack $T$, the table stack $B$, the stash $S$, the two scratch stacks $A$ and $C$ used for comparisons, and the value stack $V$.

results.title: Labels of the lookup machine
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The lookup machine has the labels $\mathsf{init}$, $\mathsf{scan}$, $\mathsf{cmp}(b)$ and $\mathsf{put}(b)$ for each bit $b$, $\mathsf{rstT}$, $\mathsf{rstB}$, $\mathsf{mvN}$, $\mathsf{back}$, $\mathsf{mark}$ and $\mathsf{done}$. The labels $\mathsf{cmp}(b)$ and $\mathsf{put}(b)$ serve a live table entry with value $b$.

results.title: Moving a symbol between stacks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For stacks $a$ and $b$, a symbol $x$ and a map $f$ from symbols to labels, this machine instruction pops the top of $a$ (if any), pushes $x$ onto $b$ and goes to the label $f(x)$.

results.title: Moving a table marker between stacks
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For stacks $a$ and $b$, a label $e$ and a map $f$ from symbols to labels, this machine instruction does the following: if the top of $a$ is a table marker $y$ (that is, $\mathsf{dead}$ or $\mathsf{val}(c)$ for a bit $c$), it pops $y$ from $a$, pushes it onto $b$ and goes to $f(y)$; if $a$ is empty or has another symbol on top, it goes to $e$ and leaves the stacks unchanged.

results.title: Next label of the lookup scan
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The label at which the lookup scan continues after moving a marker symbol $x$: the comparison label $\mathsf{cmp}(b)$ if $x$ is the value marker $\mathsf{val}(b)$, and the name-moving label $\mathsf{mvN}$ for every other symbol.

results.caption: Definition

results.caption: Definition

results.title: A name bit reads as itself
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit $b$, the name-bit symbol for $b$ reads as the bit $b$.

results.title: Initialization step of the lookup machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ and $b$ be lists of symbols and $v$ a bit. In exactly one step, the lookup program goes from the label $\mathsf{init}$ with internal bit $v$, stack $T$ holding $t$, stack $B$ holding $b$ and the stacks $S$, $A$, $C$, $V$ empty, to the label $\mathsf{scan}$ with internal bit $v$, the same contents of $T$, $B$, $S$, $A$ and $C$, and stack $V$ holding the single symbol name bit false.

results.title: Input alphabet of the SAT verifier host
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The alphabet $G$ of the host's input stack is the pair alphabet $\mathrm{Bool} \oplus \mathrm{Option}\ \mathrm{Bool}$ of the dense SAT verifier.

results.title: Stacks of the SAT verifier host
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The SAT verifier host has seventeen stacks: the input stack, the output stack, and fifteen work stacks, namely two holding the formula bits and the certificate bits, two scratch stacks used to move them in phase 0, the token and table stacks, six further stacks of the clause-check driver, two further stacks of the tokenizer, and one further stack of the 3-clause filter.

results.title: Stack alphabets of the SAT verifier host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Each stack of the SAT verifier host has an alphabet: the input stack has the input alphabet $G$, the output stack has alphabet $\mathrm{Bool}$, and every other stack has the token alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$.

results.title: Phase-0 labels of the SAT verifier host
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The five labels of phase 0 of the SAT verifier host: $m_1$ and $m_2$ move the formula bits $x$ off the input (in two passes), $\mathsf{sep}$ drops the separator, and $m_3$ and $m_4$ move the witness bits $w$ (in two passes).

results.title: Labels of the SAT verifier host
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A label of the SAT verifier host is one of the following: a phase-0 label; a label of the tokenizer; a label of the 3-clause filter; a label of the clause-check driver or of the lookup embedded in it; a cleanup label carrying an answer bit; or an output label carrying an answer bit.

results.title: Placement of the tokenizer's stacks in the host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The stacks of the tokenizer (the formula bits $X$, the witness bits $W$, the token output $T$, the table output $B$, and the clause and literal counters $CC$ and $LC$) are placed in the host machine by the map that sends each of them to the host stack of the same name.

results.title: Stack embedding of the tokenizer into the host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Every stack of the tokenizer has alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$. The tokenizer is embedded in the host machine by sending each of its stacks $X$, $W$, $T$, $B$, $CC$, $LC$ to the host stack of the same name (an injective map) and identifying the alphabet of each with that of its image, which is again $\mathrm{Sym}$, by the identity.

results.title: Placement of the lookup's stacks in the clause-check driver
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The stacks of the lookup (the query $T$, the table $B$, the stash $S$, the scratch stacks $A$ and $C$, and the value $V$) are placed in the clause-check driver by the map that sends each of them to the driver stack of the same name.

results.title: Stack embedding of the lookup into the clause-check driver
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Every stack of the lookup and of the clause-check driver has alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$. The lookup is embedded in the driver by sending each of its stacks $T$, $B$, $S$, $A$, $C$, $V$ to the driver stack of the same name (an injective map) and identifying the alphabets by the identity of $\mathrm{Sym}$.

results.title: Lookup labels in the clause-check driver
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The relabelling that places the lookup's labels among the driver's labels, whose label set consists of the driver's own labels together with the lookup's labels: the lookup's final label $\mathsf{done}$ goes to the driver's return label $\mathsf{ret}$, and every other lookup label $l$ goes to the copy of $l$ among the lookup's labels.

results.title: The embedded lookup program
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The lookup sub-program of the clause-check driver: at each lookup label $l$, it is the lookup program's statement at $l$ with every stack operation moved to the driver's stack of the same name (the lookup's stacks $T$, $B$, $S$, $A$, $C$, $V$) and every jump target relabelled by the lookup-label map, which sends $\mathsf{done}$ to the driver's return label $\mathsf{ret}$ and keeps every other label.

results.title: Driver stacks in the SAT host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The map from the stacks of the clause-check driver into the host stacks sends each driver stack to the host stack of the same name.

results.title: Stack embedding of the clause-check driver into the host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Every stack of the clause-check driver has alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$. The driver is embedded in the host machine by sending each of its stacks $T$, $B$, $S$, $A$, $C$, $V$, $P$, $F$ to the host stack of the same name (an injective map) and identifying the alphabet of each with that of its image, which is again $\mathrm{Sym}$, by the identity.

results.title: Placement of the filter's stacks in the host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The two stacks of the clause-length filter, the token stack $T$ and the side stack $U$, are placed in the host machine by the map that sends $T$ to the host stack $T$ and $U$ to the host stack $U$.

results.title: Stack embedding of the clause-length filter into the host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Both stacks of the clause-length filter have alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$. The filter is embedded in the host machine by sending its stacks $T$ and $U$ to the host stacks of the same names (an injective map) and identifying the alphabet of each with that of its image, which is again $\mathrm{Sym}$, by the identity.

results.title: Filter exits in the SAT verifier host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The relabelling of the 3-clause filter's labels into the labels of the SAT verifier host sends the filter's exit label *pass* to the start label of the clause-check driver, its exit label *fail* to the cleanup label with answer false, and every other filter label $l$ to the host's copy of $l$ among its filter labels.

results.title: Tokenizer labels in the host machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The map from labels of the tokenizer to labels of the host SAT verifier sends the tokenizer's accepting label to the start label of the embedded clause-length filter, its rejecting label to the cleanup label with answer false, and every other label $l$ to the host label that runs the tokenizer at $l$.

results.title: Driver labels in the SAT host
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The map from the labels of the clause-check driver (its own labels and those of the lookup embedded in it) to the host labels sends the driver's label for the answer yes to the cleanup label with answer true, its label for the answer no to the cleanup label with answer false, and every other label $l$ to the host label running the driver at $l$.

results.title: Explicit step bound of the SAT verifier machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a flag $\mathit{cap}$ and an input length $N$, let $s(N) = (2N + 5) + (2N + 2) + (2N + 2) + (N(8N + 9) + 1)$ be the number of steps allowed before the cleanup, and let $p$ be the per-step push budget of the host machine with that flag. results.title: SAT is in NP
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem SAT, which accepts exactly the bit strings that encode a satisfiable CNF formula, belongs to the class NP.

results.title: Cook–Levin theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: CNF satisfiability is NP-complete: the decision problem accepting exactly the bit strings that encode a satisfiable CNF formula is in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

results.title: Answer of the SAT host with the three-literal filter

The second is the return value of the SAT verifier on $(x, w)$.

results.title: 3SAT is in NP

results.title: Bit-string encoding of a graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The graph encoding of a number $n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers is the bit string that writes $n$ in unary and then, for each pair $(u, v)$ of $E$ in order, writes $u$ and then $v$ in unary, where a natural number $k$ is written in unary as $k$ ones followed by one zero.

results.title: Graph of an edge list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers, the graph of $es$ on $n$ vertices is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $es$. Loops are dropped, and pairs with an endpoint at least $n$ contribute no edge.

results.title: 3-COLOR
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem 3-COLOR accepts a bit string $x$ exactly when there are a natural number $n$ and a list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers such that $x$ is the encoding of $n$ and $es$ ($n$ in unary, then each edge $(u, v)$ as $u$ and $v$ in unary), every edge $(u, v)$ in $es$ has $u < n$ and $v < n$, and the graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with edge list $es$ (symmetrized, loops dropped) is $3$-colorable.

results.title: Consistency edges between two occurrences of a variable

results.summary: Let $l = (x, b)$ be a literal with variable index $x$ and polarity $b$, let $L$, $M$ be the vertices of a new occurrence of $l$, and let $(x', b', L', M')$ be an earlier occurrence. If $x' \ne x$ the list of consistency edges is empty. If $x' = x$ and $b' = b$ it is $[(L', M), (M', L)]$; if $x' = x$ and $b' \ne b$ it is $[(L', L), (M', M)]$.

results.title: The complete graph on four vertices as a bit string
results.caption: Definition

results.title: The SAT to 3-COLOR reduction map on bit strings
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Reading a unary number shortens the input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If reading a unary length prefix from a bit string $x$ succeeds with value $u$ and unconsumed suffix $r$, then $r$ is strictly shorter than $x$.

results.title: Edge-list decoder
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The edge-list decoder reads a bit string as a list of pairs of natural numbers, each number written in unary as that many $1$s followed by a $0$. On the empty string it returns the empty list. Otherwise it reads a number $u$, then a number $v$, decodes the rest recursively, and returns $(u, v)$ followed by the result; it fails if the input ends inside a number or after an unpaired number, or if decoding the rest…

results.title: Decoding a graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: To decode a bit string $x$, read a unary number $n$ from the front of $x$ ($n$ copies of true ended by false); if there is none, decoding fails. Otherwise decode the rest of $x$ as an edge list $es$ (pairs of unary numbers until the input ends); if that fails, decoding fails, and otherwise the result is the pair $(n, es)$.

results.title: Bit encoding of an edge list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The edge bits of a list of pairs of natural numbers are the concatenation, over its pairs $(u, v)$ in order, of $u$ ones, a zero, $v$ ones and a zero.

results.title: Decoding the empty input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The edge-list decoder, applied to the empty bit string, succeeds and returns the empty edge list.

results.title: The edge-list decoder fails on a cut-off first number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $x$ is a nonempty bit string and reading a unary length prefix from $x$ fails, then the edge-list decoder fails on $x$.

results.title: Decoding fails on a dangling half-pair
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If reading a unary length prefix from a bit string $x$ returns a number $u$ and the remaining suffix $r$, and reading a unary length prefix from $r$ fails, then the edge-list decoder fails on $x$.

results.title: Decoding one pair, then the rest
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If reading a unary length prefix from a bit string $x$ returns $u$ with remaining suffix $r$, and reading one from $r$ returns $v$ with remaining suffix $r'$, then the edge-list decoder succeeds on $x$ exactly when it succeeds on $r'$, and in that case its result on $x$ is its result on $r'$ with the pair $(u, v)$ put in front.

results.title: Decoding the bits of an edge list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers, the edge-list decoder applied to the edge bits of $es$ succeeds and returns $es$.

results.title: The edge-list decoder succeeds only on edge bits
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit string $x$ and every list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers, if the edge-list decoder returns $es$ on $x$, then $x$ is the edge bits of $es$.

results.title: Graph encoding as vertex count plus edge bits
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers, the graph encoding of $n$ and $es$ is $n$ ones, then a zero, then the edge bits of $es$.

results.title: Graph decoding inverts graph encoding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers, decoding the graph encoding of $n$ and $es$ succeeds and returns $(n, es)$.

results.title: Graph decoding succeeds only on encodings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a bit string. If decoding $x$ as a graph yields a number $n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, then $x$ is the graph encoding of $n$ and $E$.

results.title: The complete graph on four vertices is not 3-colorable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The graph on the vertices $0, 1, 2, 3$ with an edge between every two distinct vertices has no proper coloring with $3$ colors.

results.title: Proper 3-colorings of an edge list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A map $c : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1, 2\}$ properly colors a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers when $c(a) \ne c(b)$ for every pair $(a, b)$ in $E$.

results.title: 3-colorability through colorings of the natural numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and $E$ a list of pairs $(a, b)$ of natural numbers with $a < n$, $b < n$ and $a \ne b$. The graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with edge list $E$ is 3-colorable if and only if some map $c : \mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1, 2\}$ satisfies $c(a) \ne c(b)$ for every pair $(a, b)$ in $E$.

results.title: Adding a literal occurrence takes two new vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a literal $l$ and a state $s$ of the SAT-to-3-COLOR construction whose next free vertex is $n$, the state obtained by adding the occurrence $l$ to $s$ has next free vertex $n + 2$.

results.title: Growth of construction states
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A construction state $s'$ extends a construction state $s$ when the next free vertex of $s'$ is at least that of $s$, every edge emitted in $s$ is emitted in $s'$, and every occurrence recorded in $s$ is recorded in $s'$.

results.title: Extending a state makes it grow

results.title: Correctness of the reduction from SAT to 3-coloring
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A CNF formula $\varphi$ is satisfiable if and only if the graph built from $\varphi$ by the Garey–Johnson–Stockmeyer construction is 3-colorable. Here, writing $n$ for the number of vertices the construction allocates, the graph has vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, and two distinct vertices are adjacent when the construction emits an edge between them in either order.

results.title: Correctness of the SAT to 3-COLOR map on bit strings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every bit string $x$, SAT accepts $x$ if and only if 3-COLOR accepts the image of $x$ under the SAT to 3-COLOR reduction map on bit strings.

results.title: Bit encoding of an edge

results.title: Stacks of the 3-coloring emitter
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The emitter has thirteen stacks: $T$ (tokens), $O$ (output), $N$ (the next free vertex), $R$ (the current OR output), $D$ (earlier occurrences), $E$ (the walk's other side), $A$ (the current name), $P$ (its polarity), $F$ (the first-literal flag), $U$ (an earlier literal vertex), and the scratch stacks $X$ and $B$ for comparisons and $W$ for copies.

results.title: Stack alphabets of the 3-coloring emitter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The output stack has the booleans (bits) as its alphabet; every other stack has the token symbols as its alphabet.

results.title: Counters read by copy sites of the 3-COLOR emitter
results.caption: Inductive

results.title: Stack of a counter
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Unit symbol of a counter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For each of the three counters read by copy sites of the 3-coloring emitter, the unit symbol in the alphabet of the counter's stack is the clause-end token symbol.

results.title: Copy sites of the 3-COLOR emitter
results.caption: Inductive

results.title: Bit list of a copy site of the 3-COLOR emitter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a quiescent state $m$ of the 3-COLOR emitter and a copy site $j$, the bit list of $j$ at $m$ is $v$ ones followed by the constant block of $j$, where $v$ is the value in $m$ of the counter that $j$ copies. Read top-first, the ones lie above the constant block.

results.title: Running a copy site of the 3-COLOR emitter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $j$ be a copy site, $m$ a quiescent state and $v$ a local state, and let $c$ be the value in $m$ of the counter that $j$ copies. From the label that starts site $j$, with local state $v$, the machine runs in exactly $2c + 3$ steps to the label where $j$ continues, in some local state and in the quiescent state obtained from $m$ by pushing onto the output stack $c$ ones above the constant block of $j$.

results.title: Copy sites of the 3-COLOR emitter running in sequence

results.title: Color code of a vertex in a witness
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The color code of vertex $i$ in a bit string $w$ is the pair of bits at positions $2i$ and $2i + 1$ of $w$ (counting from $0$), where a position past the end of $w$ reads as $0$. The codes $00$, $01$, $10$ stand for the colors $0$, $1$, $2$; $11$ is invalid.

results.title: Valid color code
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A color code, a pair of bits $(c_1, c_2)$, is valid when it is not $11$, that is, when $c_1$ and $c_2$ are not both $1$.

results.title: The 3-COLOR verifier
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The verifier accepts an input $x$ and a witness $w$ (bit strings) iff $x$ decodes to a number $n$ and an edge list $E$, every endpoint of an edge in $E$ is less than $n$, $w$ has at least $2n$ bits, every vertex $i < n$ has a valid color code in $w$ (bits $2i$ and $2i + 1$, not $11$), and the two ends of every edge $(u, v) \in E$ with $u \ne v$ have different color codes.

results.title: Two-bit code of a color
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The code of a color $c \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ is the pair of bits whose first bit is $1$ iff $c = 2$ and whose second bit is $1$ iff $c = 1$: $0 \mapsto 00$, $1 \mapsto 01$ and $2 \mapsto 10$.

results.title: Decoding a color code
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The color in $\{0, 1, 2\}$ of a pair of bits $(a, b)$, writing $0$ for false and $1$ for true: $(0, 1)$ decodes to $1$, $(1, 0)$ decodes to $2$, and both $(0, 0)$ and the invalid code $(1, 1)$ decode to $0$.

results.title: Decoding a color code recovers the color
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every color $c \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, decoding the two-bit code of $c$ (where $0 \mapsto 00$, $1 \mapsto 01$, $2 \mapsto 10$) gives back $c$.

results.title: Color codes are valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For each color $c \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, the code of $c$ (which is $00$, $01$ or $10$) is a valid color code, that is, it is not $11$.

results.title: Re-encoding a decoded valid color
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every valid color code $c$ (a pair of bits other than $11$), the code of the color that $c$ decodes to is $c$.

results.title: Flattening pairs of bits
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The flattening of a list $[(a_1, b_1), \dots, (a_k, b_k)]$ of pairs of bits is the list of bits $[a_1, b_1, \dots, a_k, b_k]$.

results.title: Flattening the empty list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The flattening of the empty list of pairs of bits is the empty list of bits.

results.title: Flattening a nonempty list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a pair of bits $c = (a, b)$ and a list $cs$ of pairs of bits, the flattening of the list with head $c$ and tail $cs$ is the list with $a$ first, then $b$, then the flattening of $cs$.

results.title: Flattening a concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For lists $cs$ and $ds$ of pairs of bits, the flattening of the concatenation of $cs$ and $ds$ is the concatenation of the flattening of $cs$ and the flattening of $ds$.

results.title: Length of a flattening
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $cs$ of pairs of bits, the flattening of $cs$ has length $2|cs|$, two bits per pair.

results.title: Color codes of flattened pairs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $cs$ of pairs of bits and every natural number $i$, the color code of vertex $i$ in the flattening of $cs$ is the $i$-th pair of $cs$ (counting from $0$) if $i$ is less than the length of $cs$, and $00$ otherwise.

results.title: Color codes of a flattened coloring
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$, every map $f$ from $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ to pairs of bits and every $i < n$, the color code of vertex $i$ in the flattening of the list $f(0), \dots, f(n - 1)$ is $f(i)$.

results.title: 3-COLOR is verified by the witness check
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A bit string $x$ is in 3-COLOR iff some bit string $w$ of length at most $2|x|$ is accepted together with $x$ by the 3-COLOR verifier.

results.title: Witness colors of the first $n$ vertices
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a bit list $w$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the list of the color codes of the vertices $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ in $w$, in that order, where the color code of vertex $i$ is the pair of bits $2i$ and $2i+1$ of $w$ (a missing bit reads as false).

results.title: Edge verdict
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $cs$ of color codes (pairs of bits), one per vertex, and $u, v \in \mathbb{N}$, the edge $(u, v)$ passes iff $u$ and $v$ are both less than the length of $cs$ and either $u = v$ or entries $u$ and $v$ of $cs$ differ.

results.title: Edge-loop verdict
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $cs$ of color codes and a bit list $r$, the verdict is true iff $r$ parses as a list of edges, each written as two unary numbers $u$ and $v$ (a number $k$ as $k$ ones, then a zero), and every edge $(u, v)$ of that list passes the edge verdict with vertex colors $cs$.

results.title: Number of witness colors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of bits $w$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the list of the witness color codes of the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ read from $w$ has length $n$.

results.title: Reading a witness color
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a list of bits $w$ and natural numbers $i$ and $n$, write $c_w(j)$ for the color code of vertex $j$ in $w$: the pair of bits $2j$ and $2j + 1$ of $w$ (counting from $0$), each read as false past the end of $w$. If $i < n$, then entry $i$ (counting from $0$) of the list $c_w(0), \dots, c_w(n - 1)$ of witness colors is $c_w(i)$.

results.title: Peeling a vertex off the witness colors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For bits $a, b$, a bit list $w$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the color codes of the vertices $0, \dots, n$ read from the bit list $a, b, w$ (the list $w$ with $a$ and $b$ prepended) are $(a, b)$ followed by the color codes of the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ read from $w$.

results.title: The 3-COLOR verifier as an edge loop
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all bit strings $x$ and $w$, the verifier accepts $(x, w)$ iff reading a unary prefix $1^n 0$ off $x$ succeeds, giving $n$ and the rest $r$ of $x$, and then $w$ has at least $2n$ bits, each of the witness colors $c_0, \dots, c_{n-1}$ of $w$ is valid (not $11$), and the edge loop accepts $r$ with the vertex colors $c_0, \dots, c_{n-1}$.

results.title: Shifting the edge verdict past the first color
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a color code $c$, a list $cs$ of color codes and $u, v \in \mathbb{N}$, the edge verdict for $(u + 1, v + 1)$ with vertex colors $c$ followed by $cs$ equals the edge verdict for $(u, v)$ with vertex colors $cs$.

results.title: Strongly connected vertices
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a directed adjacency graph $G$, vertices $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected when $v$ is reachable from $u$ and $u$ is reachable from $v$ in $G$.

results.title: Strong connectivity is reflexive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a directed graph $G$, every vertex is strongly connected to itself.

results.title: Strong connectivity is symmetric
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a directed graph $G$, if $u$ is strongly connected to $v$, then $v$ is strongly connected to $u$.

results.title: Strong connectivity is transitive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a directed graph $G$, if $u$ is strongly connected to $v$ and $v$ is strongly connected to $w$, then $u$ is strongly connected to $w$.

results.title: Strong connectivity as an equivalence relation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a directed graph $G$, the relation on the vertices of $G$ that holds between $u$ and $v$ exactly when $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected in $G$, packaged as an equivalence relation.

results.title: Executable mutual-reachability test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a directed graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, the test returns true exactly when $v$ occurs in the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from the single root $u$, and $u$ occurs in the preorder of the depth-first search of $G$ from the single root $v$.

results.title: The mutual-reachability test is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a directed graph $G$ and vertices $u$ and $v$, the executable mutual-reachability test on $u$ and $v$ returns true if and only if $u$ and $v$ are strongly connected in $G$.

results.title: Grundy numbers of Maximum Nim
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a rule function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the Grundy number $G_f(x)$ of a pile of $x$ stones in Maximum Nim is defined by recursion on $x$ as the mex (least natural number not in the set) of $\{G_f(x - u) : 1 \le u \le \min(f(x), x)\}$, the Grundy numbers of the positions reachable from $x$ by removing $u$ stones.

results.title: Recursive formula for Maximum Nim Grundy numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every rule function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every pile size $x \in \mathbb{N}$, the Grundy number $G_f(x)$ of a pile of $x$ stones in Maximum Nim with rule function $f$ equals the mex (least natural number not in the set) of $\{G_f(x - u) : 1 \le u \le \min(f(x), x)\}$.

results.title: Grundy number of a pile of four in halving Maximum Nim

results.title: Grundy number of a pile of three in halving Maximum Nim

results.title: The Maximum Nim game
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a rule function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the Maximum Nim game with rule $f$ is the impartial game whose positions are the pile sizes $x \in \mathbb{N}$, in which the moves from $x$ go to $x - u$ for each $u$ with $1 \le u \le \min(f(x), x)$. The rank of a position is the pile size itself, and the starting position is the empty pile $0$.

results.title: P-positions of Maximum Nim
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a rule function and let $x$ be a pile size. The position $x$ of the Maximum Nim game with rule $f$ is a P-position if and only if, for every $u$ with $1 \le u \le \min(f(x), x)$, the position $x - u$ is not a P-position.

results.title: Grundy number where the rule function increases
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $f(0) = 0$ and $f(m-1) \le f(m) \le f(m-1) + 1$ for every $m \ge 1$, and let $G$ be the Grundy number of Maximum Nim with rule function $f$. If $x \ge 1$ and $f(x-1) < f(x)$, then $G(x) = f(x)$.

results.title: Grundy number where the rule function is flat
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $f(0) = 0$ and $f(m-1) \le f(m) \le f(m-1) + 1$ for every $m \ge 1$, and let $G$ be the Grundy number of Maximum Nim with rule function $f$. If $x \ge 1$ and $f(x) = f(x-1)$, then $G(x) = G(x - f(x) - 1)$.

results.title: Maximum Nim Grundy numbers at non-multiples of the divisor

results.title: Alignment
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An alignment over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a finite list of columns, where each column is a pair $(u, v)$ and each of $u$ and $v$ is either a letter of $\alpha$ or a gap.

results.title: Valid alignment of two sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A list $A$ of columns, each a pair of optional letters, is an alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$ when no column has both entries empty, the letters present in the first entries of the columns, read in order, form $x$, and the letters present in the second entries, read in order, form $y$.

results.title: Score of an alignment column
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma$, which assigns an integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to all letters $a, b \in \alpha$, and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, a column pairing letters $a$ and $b$ scores $\sigma(a, b)$, a column pairing a letter with a gap (on either side) scores $g$, and a column with a gap on both sides scores $0$.

results.title: Score of an alignment
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a substitution score $\sigma$, which assigns an integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to all letters $a, b \in \alpha$, and a gap score $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, the score of an alignment $A$ over $\alpha$ is the sum, over all columns of $A$, of the score of the column with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$.

results.title: Concatenation of alignments

results.title: The list of all alignments

results.title: The enumerated alignments are exactly the valid ones
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For sequences $x$ and $y$ and a list $A$ of columns, $A$ occurs in the enumerated list of all alignments of $x$ and $y$ if and only if $A$ is an alignment of $x$ and $y$.

results.title: Needleman–Wunsch is optimal

results.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$ and every valid alignment $A$ of $x$ and $y$, the score of $A$ with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$ is at most the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.

results.title: Needleman–Wunsch is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma : \alpha \to \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a substitution score and $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ a gap score. For all sequences $x$ and $y$ over $\alpha$ there is a valid alignment $A$ of $x$ and $y$ whose score with respect to $\sigma$ and $g$ equals the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.

results.title: The terminal Smith–Waterman cell is nonnegative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every substitution score $\sigma$, every gap score $g$ and all sequences $x$ and $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell $H(x, y)$ satisfies $H(x, y) \ge 0$.

results.title: The terminal cell vanishes when the first sequence is empty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap score $g$ and every sequence $y$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell of the empty sequence and $y$ is $0$.

results.title: The terminal cell vanishes when the second sequence is empty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a substitution score $\sigma$, a gap score $g$ and every sequence $x$, the terminal Smith–Waterman cell of $x$ and the empty sequence is $0$.
